messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Another crash problem
parts:
Dear experts

For a large, but relatively simple model with only fixed effects, the following message appears after the INLA-call:

Error in if (any(i < 0L)) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message:
In int2i(as.integer(i), n) : NAs introduced by coercion to integer range

Perhaps I am to blame myself for giving bad input, but if I divide the data in two parts and run them separately, both parts run smooth.

What has happened here?

best
Øyvind

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another crash problem
parts:
You are right, Håvard, but how did they get there?


inla.spde.make.index is not to blame

> spde.y$n.spde
[1] 1260
> id.y.s = inla.spde.make.index(name = "fld.y.s", n.spde = spde.y$n.spde)
>
> tail(id.y.s$fld.y.s)
[1] 1255 1256 1257 1258 1259 1260

the NAs arise in inla.stack.data:

> tail(inla.stack.data(stack3.yY)$fld.y.s)
[1] NA NA NA NA NA NA

with stack3.yY defined as: 

> stack3.y = inla.stack(data = list(y = cbind(dat.i$y, rep(NA, n.i), rep(NA, n.i)), weights = dat.i$ca/weights0, scale = scale.ca.i), 
+ A = list(A.y.s, A.y.st, 1), 
+ effects = list(id.y.s, id.y.st, data.frame(y.const = rep(1,n.i), y.time = dat.i$time, y.p = dat.i$p, y.par = dat.i$par, y.d_k = dat.i$d_k, y.d_r = dat.i$d_r, y.d_m = dat.i$d_m, y.d_s = dat.i$d_s, y.d_g = dat.i$d_g, y.alt = dat.i$alt, y.age = dat.i$age)), 
+ tag = "stack.y")
> 
> stack3.Y = inla.stack(data = list(y = cbind(dat.k$Y, rep(NA, n.k), rep(NA, n.k)), weights = dat.k$CA/weights0, scale = scale.CA.k), 
+ A = list(A.k.y.s, A.k.y.st, 1), 
+ effects = list(id.y.s, id.y.st, data.frame(y.const = rep(1,n.k), y.time = dat.k$time, y.p = dat.k$P, y.par = dat.k$y.par, y.d_k = dat.k$y.d_k, y.d_r = dat.k$y.d_r, y.d_m = dat.k$y.d_m, y.d_s = dat.k$y.d_s, y.d_g = dat.k$y.d_g, y.alt = dat.k$y.alt, y.age = dat.k$y.age)), 
+ tag = "stack.Y")
> 
> stack3.yY = inla.stack(stack3.y, stack3.Y)
>

Of course, I can make a simpler stack and possibly come around the problem, but what are the mistakes in my stack command?


best Øyvind

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another crash problem
parts:
Further to Daniel's question of what your stacks are intended to do:
1) the whole point of inla.stack is to join things together with NA:s in the required places, so NA:s in there is expected.
2) both stacks have three column data matrices where the same two last columns are completely full of NA in both stacks. If you run a multi-likelihood model I would expect that to be a problem, as there would be no data whatsoever. If you only have one likelihood, use a vector instead.

Finn

messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Another crash problem
parts:
Dear Daniel and Finn

My stack is part of larger 3-likelihood model. I run only the first likelihood to check if it is ok. There are also spatial indices in this stack that are not used for the model here. They are invoked in other models. On purpose I construct the stacks general so that they apply to several models. This simplifies modeling and will hopefully reduce the number of mistakes.

In all cases the simple model has been running smoothly except for this large case, which is not even accepted by inla. Hence, your explanation does not seem to apply, Finn. Actually, a slightly different program of same size with a different index (which actually is not even used in the model) runs smoothly.

I am inclined to think that I have exceeded some internal limits of the stack program by writing a stack command beyond what you conceive sensible persons to do. If so, I would like to know what these limits are.

best
Øyvind







As a programmer I appreciate such events as they may point to errorscan of cou

Dear Daniel and Finn

My stack is part of larger 3-likelihood model. I run only the first likelihood to check if it is ok. There are also spatial indices in this stack that are not used for the model here. They are invoked in other models. On purpose I construct the stacks general so that they apply to several models. This simplifies modeling and will hopefully reduce the number of mistakes.

In all cases the simple model has been running smoothly except for this large case, which is not even accepted by inla. Hence, your explanation does not seem to apply, Finn. Actually, a slightly different program of same size with a different index (which actually is not even used in the model) runs smoothly.

I am inclined to think that I have exceeded some internal limits of the stack program by writing a stack command beyond what you conceive sensible persons to do. If so, I would like to know what these limits are.

fredag 31. mars 2017 10.47.22 UTC+2 skrev Finn Lindgren følgende:
Further to Daniel's question of what your stacks are intended to do:
1) the whole point of inla.stack is to join things together with NA:s in the required places, so NA:s in there is expected.
2) both stacks have three column data matrices where the same two last columns are completely full of NA in both stacks. If you run a multi-likelihood model I would expect that to be a problem, as there would be no data whatsoever. If you only have one likelihood, use a vector instead.

Finn
